## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Karim and Ingrid both ask to see it work on their own phone numbers before paying, so they belong together under a plain name, while Andreas (the licence costs more than the few lost bookings) and Hannes (no robot at any price) make different points and rightly stand alone.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all four speak to what it would take to be worth paying for.

founder.order_why: Mostly logical, but 'Offer a pilot?' (22) comes after I had already set my first step as paying €3,000 for a pilot at one hotel (20-21), so it belongs next to the commitment step, not at the end.
founder.asked_twice: 20/21 (first step: pay €3,000 for a pilot at one hotel) and 22 (Offer a pilot?) both ask about the pilot; 3 and 4 also repeat the same context question across two screens.
founder.missing: No place to say that the pilot is money-back and that its fee is credited to the licence on roll-out, which is the core of my offer. Nothing asks for call volume or number of hotels per group, which are needed to turn 'miss 5% of calls' into euros lost.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It moves sensibly from how many calls we lose, to what it's worth, to budget, sign-off, data protection and then the pilot, and the follow-up on timing sits right after the answer it picks up on.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.asked_twice: Screens 6 and 7 partly overlap: both are about how long it would take, though 7 asks what fills that time.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: How we cover unanswered and after-hours calls today and what that costs us; whether it connects to our CRS/PMS and books directly; how good it is at handling guests in German; and the contract terms after the pilot.

screens.why1: Right after I named who has to agree, it makes sense to show me the list Keel built so I can check it before it becomes the belief strangers test.
screens.why2: Reservation agent, revenue director, the hotel's owner, has the problem, decides to buy, has to agree are all words I use every day selling to hotel groups.
screens.why3: Who books the calls, who signs for a hotel group and whose agreement the director needs is exactly what I deal with on every sales call.
screens.why4: The rows are distinct and well tagged, but 'The finance director' is a row I never put there, so one option is odd.
screens.why5: My agent, my director and the hotel's owner are kept as I said them, but a finance director has crept in as 'has to agree' even though the intro claims Keel used only the roles I named.
screens.why7: The shape holds (Nobody else first, agent tagged with the problem, director tagged as deciding, at most two tagged has to agree, every row tagged, 4 words each), but the card's 'Keel adds none' rule is bent by a finance director I never named, which would put a second role I never claimed into the belief.
screens.instead: The people involved: Nobody else · Reservation agent · has the problem · Hotel group revenue director · decides to buy · The hotel's owner · has to agree -- reword, remove or add up to one more who has to agree.

screens.why1: Right after I named who has to agree and checked Keel's rows, choosing which belief to put to the revenue directors is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Owner, finance director and sign-off are everyday words in a German hotel group, and the intro says plainly that the decider gets one question about who else has to agree.
screens.why3: I know how a purchase goes through at the groups I sell to, so I can pick this from my own deals without guessing.
screens.why4: The two choices cover my options, but the owner and the finance director are fused into one row, so I cannot pick the owner alone, which is the role I actually hold has to agree.
screens.why5: I said the hotel's owner has to agree; the finance director sitting beside the owner as a co-equal must-agree drifts from my answer, and the file's item is the owner alone.
screens.why7: The belief joins every has-to-agree role with 'and', and the bar can be both supported and refuted, but the card's shape asks for one row per role and here the two roles share one row.
screens.instead: Which one do you want to test? · Nobody else · The hotel's owner · has to agree · The finance director · has to agree -- test: The hotel group revenue director decides, and the hotel's owner must agree first.

screens.why1: Right after naming who has to agree, asking what the hotel group must clear before paying is the natural next step in how it sells.
screens.why2: "The buyer's own side" is Keel's abstraction; screen 14 already called them the hotel group revenue director, so I need the hint to be sure it means the group's own approvals, like a data protection review.
screens.why3: I sell to German hotel groups and know the data protection review of guest calls, plus the owner's sign-off, is what stalls my deals.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in with only "I'm not sure" as the escape, which fits a founder who might not know the buyer's process.
screens.why5: My answer "A data protection review of guest calls" sits in the box exactly as I typed it.
screens.why7: The box asks for 1 to 4 buyer-side steps of at most 9 words, biggest first, excludes my own trial or pilot, and says I pick one and give its time next; my data protection review is a real brake on the buyer's side, the kind the card names.
screens.instead: What must a hotel group clear on its own side before it can pay for Codyco (for example a data protection review or the owner's sign-off)? Up to four steps, biggest first, not your own pilot.

screens.why1: Right after I named what the buyer's side must clear, Keel shows me what it saved so I can check it before I pick one and give it a time; that is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: A data protection review and a works council (Betriebsrat) review are the plain words of any German hotel group's head office, and the intro is short and clear.
screens.why3: I sell to German hotel groups; I know the DSGVO review of recorded guest calls and the Betriebsrat's say over a system that touches how agents handle calls are real gates I meet in deals.
screens.why4: Two distinct steps on the buyer's own side: one is the guests' data, the other is the staff's representation; neither overlaps the other, and my own blocker comes first.
screens.why5: My row is kept word for word, and Keel's addition is tagged and doesn't put my pilot, price or roles into the list.
screens.why7: Both rows are buyer-side brakes I don't control, each a noun phrase with its object under 9 words; my step is first; Keel added only one row, the works council gate that this trade in Germany actually imposes; nothing is my offer, a pilot or the purchase itself; and no time is prefilled, so the time stays mine for the Choose screen.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the steps, I pick the one to test and say how long I expect it to take, which is the obvious next move.
screens.why2: A data protection review of guest calls and a works council review are exactly the words a German hotel group's director uses, and the time box is plain.
screens.why3: I know from selling to German hotel groups that the data protection officer has to look at recorded guest calls, so I can name a time from my own deals.
screens.why4: Two distinct steps on the buyer's side, both real German gates, in my trade's words, with 'I'm not sure' as the fitting escape.
screens.why5: My step is kept word for word as the first row, and the belief carries the 4 weeks I typed myself, not a time Keel chose.
screens.why7: Both rows are brakes on the buyer's side rather than my pilot or the purchase itself. My own row comes first, Keel adds only one suggestion, and it is the works council gate this trade and place really impose. The time is mine, and the bar (at least 2 in 3 under 4 weeks or not needed) can both hold and fail. The escape is there.

screens.why1: After who decides, the price and what the buyer's side must clear, asking for the first real step is the obvious close of the commercial part, and the €3,000 pilot is exactly what I lead with.
screens.why2: Pilot, trial and paying for it are my everyday sales words; the question and its 9-word hint read on first pass.
screens.why3: The first step is my own offer, the money-back pilot at one hotel in my partnership terms, so I answer it from what I know.
screens.why4: The only chip is the escape, and 'I'm not sure' fits a founder who has no step in mind, matching the card's rule that it leaves the dimension out.
screens.why5: My answer goes in as I typed it, keeping €3,000, money-back and one hotel, and nothing on the screen reworded it.
screens.why7: The box asks for one step in base form, at most 9 words, naming where the money goes and promising a smaller free step only when it costs money, data or a signature; my 9-word step meets all of that and will fill 'Yes, I'd {step}' whole.

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first real step, this screen shows how strangers will hear it before the commercial part closes, which is exactly where it belongs.
screens.why2: The step and the four answers read plainly to me as a founder selling to hotel groups, but the smaller-step field shows 'Yes, after a demo using example calls first', with the answer's frame still on it, so I have to read it twice to see that the step itself is just 'a demo using example calls'.
screens.why3: A revenue director at a German hotel group signs off on pilots like this, so whether they would pay €3,000 for one hotel is a question they can answer from their own work.
screens.why4: The four options cover a firm yes to the paid pilot, a soft yes after a free demo, probably not and no; they are distinct and nothing is missing.
screens.why5: My €3,000, the money-back term and the one-hotel scope are all kept within the nine words, and the free demo with example calls is a fair smaller step that I would keep.
screens.why7: The first option is my step whole and the soft yes is a yes to it after a free demo that takes no money, data or signature; the list is two for and two against with no escape, so the belief can hold or fail.
screens.instead: Show the smaller step as 'a demo using example calls' (without 'Yes, after ... first'); keep the four options as they are.

screens.why1: Right after I set the first real step, and before strangers see the study, it is obvious why Keel asks whether to put a pilot offer at the end.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with yes/no and a one-line hint showing exactly what the respondent will see is plain to me on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I want leads from the study is my own call as the founder, and I already run a pilot programme, so I can answer it straight away.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers the choice, the two options are distinct and the wording is plain.
screens.why5: My step was "pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel", but the line respondents get is a generic "Would you try this for real? Leave your email", which drops the paid, money-back, one-hotel pilot I typed one screen earlier.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Hint: People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one of your hotels? Leave your email." Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who will put the questions to people belongs right here, just before the study goes out and after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain: two named voices, a five-second sample of each, a fixed 400-credit cost and a link sent by text.
screens.why3: As the founder I can judge which voice my reservation agents in Munich would listen to after a five-second sample.
screens.why4: The two voices are distinct, but nothing says whether either one asks in German, which is the answer that matters for agents at German hotel groups.
screens.why5: It says only 'reservation agents', but this study's commercial part also goes to revenue directors, and the hint speaks of a voice while my recorded pick speaks of a face.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents and revenue directors your questions, in German? Daphne (German) ▶ Hear · 5 s / Saskia (German) ▶ Hear · 5 s

screens.why1: Right after choosing how reservation agents are asked, it is obvious that the revenue directors on the commercial link need their own format chosen too.
screens.why2: AI interviewer, read and tap, or let them choose are plain to me, and each comes with a one-line description of what the director will see.
screens.why3: I know my directors are busy people who open a link between meetings, so I can judge which format they would answer in.
screens.why4: The three options cover the choices, they are distinct, and my pick 'Read and tap' is there; only the third option's 'Daphne or text' names the second option differently from its label.
screens.why5: 'Directors' is my revenue or reservations director, and nothing of Codyco leaks into the format choice.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how directors answer, deciding who receives the link is the natural last step before sending, and I'd send it to the hotel-group revenue directors I already know from our 7 groups and pipeline.
screens.why2: The three options are plain to me; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own page, which I've seen in the app, and 'signs in with Google' is clear.
screens.why3: I know exactly whom I can reach (directors I know by name) versus whether I'd post in a hotelier group, so I can answer from my own situation.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover the cases, but the screen doesn't say whether this is for the directors' link or the reservation agents' one, and it offers no way to combine named people with an open link.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is altered; it's a plain distribution choice and my pick, people I know by name, is kept.
screens.instead: Who gets the revenue directors' link? People I know by name (a link each) / People from a Contacts search / One open link I post where hotel directors already are (e.g. a hotelier LinkedIn group) / Some of each

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Did not hold' sits right beside the number that decides it, Purchase friction at 4 of 8 under 4 weeks against a bar of 6, and it matches the 'worst card' rule printed below.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows its count and its bar ('bar 6 of 8 · 2 short'), but 'Ability to pay · 5 needed' and the kicker's '4 TO 8 COUNTED' need a second look before I know what was counted over whom.
screens.why_b3: Most beliefs are in my own words (the 5% of calls, €3,000 up front, the money-back pilot at one hotel, the data protection review of guest calls), but Buyer and payer adds 'the finance director must agree' when I only said the owner has to agree.
screens.why_b4: The only line under the verdict says who the money questions went to; nothing says what the data protection result or the short price means for my pilot offer or what to do about it.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, but it is never called a small sample, and Price and Existing sacrifice, which are both short of their bars, are labelled 'People disagree' rather than short, which softens two misses.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 4 of 8 directors expect the data protection review of guest calls to take 4 weeks to 3 months, and only 4 of 8 would pay €3,000 up front; only 8 directors answered, so ship a ready GDPR/data-processing pack with the money-back pilot and test the price again.

screens.why_b1: The status 'People disagree, a split' sits right beside its deciding number: 4 of 7 at 5% or more against a bar of 5 of 7, 1 short.
screens.why_b2: The strip says it counts % of the reservation calls a month, one cell per person over 7 counted, with my 5% marked and the bar of 5 of 7 named, though 'bar' sitting next to a 5% marker and a 5-of-7 threshold takes half a beat to separate.
screens.why_b3: It is my 5% of the reservation calls per hotel a month and my loss line, booking calls that rang out unanswered, in my words, even if the line drops 'hotel groups' as the ones it costs.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and hands me to the Price card; it never says what a 1-short split means for my 5% pitch, such as that the groups with a call center sit below it and the resort and peak groups above.
screens.why_b5: n is visible throughout, Karim's 'can't recall' and Hannes's none-as-0 are both explained, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps the split from being oversold either way.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 groups lose 5% or more of their calls, 1 short of the bar; the 3 below have a call center or quiet season, so pitch the 5% to groups without after-hours cover and lead the pilot there.

screens.why_b1: The deciding number (4 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, 2 short) is on the screen, but the status word says 'People disagree a split' rather than 'did not hold', so the verdict is not plainly tied to a missed bar.
screens.why_b2: The up-front chart reads cleanly with my €3,000 on a band edge, but the monthly chart only adds up to 7 people and its strip shows 4 for and 3 against, so I have to work out that Hannes's would-not-pay is missing there.
screens.why_b3: My numbers are kept, but my €3,000 was a money-back pilot at one location credited on roll-out, and the belief and question turn it into a plain 'per hotel, once' fee, which drops the terms I attached.
screens.why_b4: The So line only sends me to the Insights tab; it does not say whether to lower the licence, make the pilot free, or aim at groups with a higher missed-call rate.
screens.why_b5: It says 'a small group: a lean, not a call' and keeps n visible, but the second strip's 3 against disagrees with the 4 short in the verdict line, which softly misstates the monthly side.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 4 of 8 would pay a €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel and €1,000+ a month per hotel, short of 6 of 8; the ones below lose under 5% of calls or cannot see their rate, so show them their missed calls before quoting the pilot.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed', and the So line repeats the same reason.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts money sources across the 4 directors at my price, but I had to work out that 'your bar · 4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3)' means 4 'for' out of a 5-person floor, with the ghost cell as the missing fifth director.
screens.why_b3: It names the revenue director as the payer and uses my own €3,000 pilot and €1,000 to €1,500 licence, so this is my price and my buyer in my numbers.
screens.why_b4: 'Waits until 5 have' tells me the card is blocked, but not to reach one more director at my price, or that the 3-for, 1-against lean is behind a Price split that matters more.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n visible and calls the result 'a lean, not a call', but the rule line counts against 'none', which is not an option, and leaves out 'charged to the teams or sites' (for) and 'a grant' (against), so the rule does not match the chart.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 directors at my price would pay from a budget line they already have, and 1 needs a new one. Reach one more director who would pay €3,000 to settle it, but the real block is that only 4 of 8 took my price.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its number, 6 of 8 as I said or easier against a bar of 6 of 8, so I know it held, and only just.
screens.why_b2: The four bars carry their counts and for/against tags in the item's own order, and the strip shows 6 for and 2 against over 8 with the marker at 6, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is mine and the revenue director with the owner is my belief, but the belief line adds 'the finance director', whom I never named, and the bar line beneath it says only 'You said the hotel's owner has to agree', so the card disagrees with itself about what I said.
screens.why_b4: 'Plan for the hotel's owner in most deals; 2 of 8 could sign alone' tells me concretely to build the owner's sign-off into my pilot sales, and to expect a few directors to sign alone.
screens.why_b5: It says n=8 and 'a lean, not a call', but 'Holding up' under a belief that names the finance director overstates what was asked, since the item only asked about the owner and the finance director was never tested.
screens.instead: Belief: The hotel group revenue director decides, and the hotel's owner must agree first. Holding up 6 of 8 (bar 6), a lean from 8 people. Plan for the owner's sign-off on the €3,000 pilot.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside its deciding number, "4 of 8 under 4 weeks or not needed · bar 6 of 8 · 2 short", so I see at once that my 4 weeks lost and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The bands show their counts and for/against marks over 8 people, the strip puts the marker at 6, and the note that my 4 weeks is the low edge of the 4-weeks-to-3-months band explains why that band counts against me.
screens.why_b3: The data protection review of guest calls is the step I picked for German hotels handling guests' card and personal data, and the belief names it with my 4 weeks; only the bar line "You said a data protection review of guest calls" drops the time.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for a review of 4 weeks to 3 months before a group signs, which matters to my €3,000 pilot pitch, and points me to Insights for what eats the time.
screens.why_b5: All 8 answers are listed and counted, the count line says "a small group: a lean, not a call", and the 4/4 split is stated plainly without inflating it.
screens.instead: You said a data protection review of guest calls would take about 4 weeks; 4 of 8 expect 4 weeks to 3 months, so have your data processing agreement and GDPR pack ready before the pilot pitch.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside 6 of 8 said yes, bar 6 of 8, at the bar, so I know the belief held and by exactly how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over the 8 directors, the strip shows 6 for and 2 against, and the marker sits at 6, so all three are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: Commitment and "pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel" are my step word for word, and the hotel group revenue director is the person I named as deciding.
screens.why_b4: "Book them into it" is concrete: put the six yeses on a paid pilot at one hotel this month.
screens.why_b5: The count line does say "a lean, not a call", but "Holding up" and the flat "would pay … Book them into it" never say that the result sits exactly on the bar and one answer flips it to Did not hold, which is a soft overstatement for a yes said on a survey.
screens.instead: 6 of 8 said they'd pay €3,000 for the money-back pilot. That is exactly at the bar, and one more no would sink it, so book those six into a paid pilot now and count it only when the money lands.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its status word with the deciding count beside it (Price 4 of 8 against a bar of 6, Purchase friction 4 of 8 with 2 short, Buyer and payer 6 of 8 at the bar), so I know where each line landed.
screens.why_b3: Price and the data protection review are my words, but the Buyer and payer belief adds a finance director next to the owner, which I recognise but did not quite say.
screens.why_b4: Under 'When a line fails' the screen gives only quotes; it never says what the failed Price and Purchase friction lines mean for the €3,000 pilot or what I should change.
screens.why_b5: Price sits 2 short of its bar and is softened to 'People disagree' rather than called not held, and the Purchase friction box is empty with no word that its failure is unexplained, though n and the never-saw names stay visible.
screens.why_b6: Karim and Ingrid wanting a free test on their own numbers first, and Andreas working out that at 4% across nine hotels the licence costs more than the bookings it saves, tell me something I did not type: the price has to be proven against each group's own miss rate.

screens.why1: As the first screen of a link about buying a booking tool, showing me the idea before any questions on it is exactly where it belongs.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot, Apaleo, calls handed to the desk by rules: that is my daily vocabulary as a revenue director running a reservations office.
screens.why3: Missed calls after hours and at peak, payment on the phone and bookings landing in our PMS are things I see and pay for every week.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but the belief line only repeats the opening line word for word, so it no longer says what the founder believes the tool would change for me.
screens.why6: Short sentences that say well over the phone; PMS is spoken as letters in my trade, and the system names are just a short list of three.
screens.instead: Keep the card, but end it with: The people building it believe no booking call would go unanswered, at night, at peak or on holidays.

screens.why1: Straight after the idea, asking what share of booking calls we already miss is the obvious first question for the person who pays for the reservations office.
screens.why2: I can work out that it means our unanswered rate, but 'go without in booking calls that rang out' says the calls twice and needs a second read; we just say unanswered or abandoned calls.
screens.why3: Our phone system reports the unanswered rate every month, and I know ours runs around 6%.
screens.why4: A percent box labelled with the base and the month, a None for zero and a single 'I can't recall' cover every answer I could give.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but 'go without' is not how anyone in reservations talks about missed calls, so the founder's plain 'unanswered calls' has drifted.
screens.why6: It is one question within 20 words with one escape, but 'go without in booking calls that rang out unanswered' is a tangle to hear once.
screens.why7: The measure, base and period match a percent of reservation calls a month and both sides stay open, but the item names the thing twice and uses 'go without' where the writer could have said 'rang out unanswered'.
screens.instead: Last month, about what percent of your reservation calls rang out unanswered? [ box ] % of reservation calls last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after the Codyco card and the question on missed calls, asking what it would be worth to me as the one who pays is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Up front, per hotel' and 'a month, per hotel' are how a setup fee and a monthly licence are put to me by every booking-tool vendor, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I sign off on these tools per property and know what a lost booking call costs us, so I can give a real figure rather than a guess.
screens.why4: Both ladders are complete and distinct, with no amount in two bands, a clear 'wouldn't pay' answer, and 'I can't say' kept apart as the escape.
screens.why5: Only the idea's own name, Codyco, reaches me, as shown on the card, and nothing of the founder's plan or their words for people leaks into the bands.
screens.why6: Each step reads four short options I can hold, followed by a two-choice follow-up, with the one escape said once per question; the euro figures say naturally as 'three thousand euros'.
screens.why7: This is a one-price-first-then-plan offer served as two ladders of six on the one measure (euros per hotel, up front, then monthly), each with two bands below a middle edge and three from it, plus 'I wouldn't pay for this' and the 'I can't say' escape, so the belief can be both supported and refuted.

screens.why1: Right after I named a price, asking where that money would come from is the obvious next step for the person who signs the budget.
screens.why2: Budget line, charged to the sites, signed off: this is how I talk about money every month, and I can answer at first reading.
screens.why3: I know exactly how a new reservations tool gets paid for in our group, so I answer from what I do, not a guess.
screens.why4: The five sources are distinct and cover my real answer, charging it back to the hotels that use it; a grant is unlikely for us but is a real source (Digital Jetzt and similar), and 'I can't say' fits as the one escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the price restated here drops the 'per hotel' that screen 3 asked in, so I briefly wonder whether €3,000 to €5,000 is the group total or per property.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it is one short question pointing back to my price, then five short options I can hold, and one escape said last.
screens.why7: Every option is a source of money that reads after 'would', there are three for and two against in the card's order, and the single 'I can't say' sits apart as the card requires.
screens.instead: You said about €3,000 to €5,000 up front per hotel, then €1,000 to €2,500 a month. If you went ahead at that, where would the money come from? (same five options, 'Charged to the hotels that use it' for the second; I can't say)

screens.why1: Right after I said where the money would come from, asking whether I can approve it myself or need the owner is the obvious next step in the buying conversation.
screens.why2: Sign off and owner are my everyday words, but 'about €3,000 per hotel' drops the 'up front' and the monthly €1,000 to €2,500 I just gave, so I'd pause to check whether it means the one-off alone or the whole deal.
screens.why3: I know my own approval limits and when a property's owner or our Geschäftsführung has to agree, so I can answer this from how we actually buy.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone to someone else's decision, each opens differently, and our managing director or a CFO-plus-owner setup still fits 'several people' or 'someone else's call', with I can't say apart.
screens.why5: The hotel's owner is a plain role in my trade, given the management contracts groups like mine run under, and nothing of the product's pitch or the founder's own terms comes through.
screens.why6: One short either-or question, four short parallel options said as a list I can hold, and the single escape said last; the euro figure says well as 'about three thousand euros'.
screens.why7: All four options sit on the one measure of who has to agree; they are in order from alone to someone else's call with the founder's role (the hotel's owner) in the second; For (decided alone, owner agrees) and Against (several, someone else's) can both occur; I can't say is the one escape, shown apart.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about €3,000 per hotel up front yourself, or would the hotel's owner have to agree? I could sign off myself · The hotel's owner would have to agree · Several people would have to agree · It's someone else's call · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off myself, it makes sense to ask what else stands between us and buying, and for a German hotel group taking guest calls, data protection is the obvious next gate.
screens.why2: A data protection review of guest calls is exactly what our Datenschutzbeauftragter would run on anything that listens to or records reservation calls, so I understand it on first reading.
screens.why3: I have taken call-center and CRM tools through our data protection officer, and often the works council too, so I can give a real estimate of how long this one would take.
screens.why4: The bands run from short to long without gaps or overlaps, 'It wouldn't be needed' is a real answer, and 'I can't tell' fits as the escape, though '4 weeks to 3 months' mixes weeks and months a little.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's pitch reaches me beyond the named product from the idea card, and the step is said in the words my trade uses.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it is one short question with four options, then a two-option follow-up, which I can hold and answer at once.
screens.why7: Every option measures the step's own time, five bands have one edge at the founder's 4 weeks plus 'It wouldn't be needed', both sides can win, the step is a real brake on my side, and 'I can't tell' is the only escape.

screens.why1: I just said the data protection review would take 4 weeks to 3 months, so asking what would eat that time is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: It plays back my answer the way I'd say it, "4 weeks to 3 months", and asks in plain words what would hold it up.
screens.why3: I know exactly what drags this out here: our data protection officer, the works council on recording staff calls, and a data processing agreement with a new vendor, so I can answer from my own experience.
screens.why4: A free-text box with no options.
screens.why5: It asks about buying Codyco under the name I was shown on the idea card, and nothing of the founder's own terms comes through.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, no symbols or abbreviations, easy to take in once over the phone.
screens.instead: You said 4 weeks to 3 months. What would take the time in the data protection review of guest calls?

screens.why1: After price, budget, sign-off and the data protection review, asking whether I'd actually put money on a pilot is the obvious last question of the buying section.
screens.why2: A money-back pilot at one hotel for €3,000 is exactly how I'd talk about trialling a reservations tool, and a demo with example calls is plain to anyone running a reservations office.
screens.why3: I'm the one who decides and pays for tools like this across our hotels, so whether I'd fund a one-hotel pilot is my call to answer.
screens.why4: Firm yes, a yes after a free demo, probably not and no cover what I'd really say, with no overlap and nothing missing.
screens.why5: The founder's pilot keeps its price, its money-back term and its one-hotel scope, and nothing of how they run it reaches me beyond the idea card I was meant to see.
screens.why6: One short question and four options I can hold after hearing them once; 'three thousand euros' says cleanly and the long first option just repeats the question.
screens.why7: The first option is the founder's own costed step word for word; the second is a yes to it after a free demo that costs no money, data or signature; the 2-for and 2-against balance has no escape, and 'Most would pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot' can be held or refuted.
